thread.title_full: Opinion: 'Taming' the military in the name of civilian control - NewsBreak

author: Asia Today and translated by UPI
title: Opinion: 'Taming' the military in the name of civilian control - NewsBreak
text:
By Asia Today and translated by UPI ,
6 hours ago March 11 (Asia Today) -- This commentary is the Asia Today Editor's Op-Ed.
Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back speaks during a press conference at the defense ministry in Seoul, South Korea, 12 February 2026, to announce the findings of an investigation into former President Yoon Suk Yeol’s short-lived martial law bid in late 2024. Photo by YONHAP / EPA South Korea's defense minister emphasized political neutrality and civilian control of the military when he took office last July. But recent developments have raised concerns that those principles may be used to reshape the armed forces to suit political interests.
In his inaugural address, Defense Minister Ahn Kyu-baek said the military must operate according to the Constitution and laws reflecting the will of the people. He also stressed that the armed forces must strictly maintain political neutrality and focus solely on protecting the nation from external threats.
Yet critics say the slogan of civilian control may now be serving as justification for political pressure on the military.
The Ministry of National Defense recently imposed a one-month suspension on Adm. Kang Dong-gil, the navy's top officer whom the government itself appointed. At a disciplinary hearing, Kang reportedly argued that certain actions were illegal and said he issued instructions to subordinate units to prevent additional troop deployments.
Despite those claims, the ministry disciplined the four-star admiral for what it described as a violation of duty, effectively forcing him from his post.
Concerns have also grown over a second special investigation related to the Dec. 3 emergency martial law incident. Within the military, some officers say investigators are again targeting key institutions and individuals, including those previously cleared in the first inquiry.
Critics say the investigation has even extended to mid-level officers who had no role in policy decisions, raising questions about whether soldiers can be held responsible for carrying out orders later deemed unlawful.
South Korea's military has long lacked a clear legal framework protecting the right to refuse unlawful orders, though legislation is now under consideration.
Holding individual officers solely responsible for illegal directives, critics argue, risks turning the investigation into a sweeping purge rather than a fair inquiry.
The debate also raises broader questions about national security. With North Korea's nuclear threat continuing, some observers warn that targeting senior commanders and treating future leaders as potential criminals could undermine morale across the armed forces.
Military morale, they say, is built not on financial incentives but on honor and trust. If soldiers fear punishment for carrying out orders from superiors, they may hesitate to act decisively in times of crisis.
The core purpose of civilian control and political neutrality, critics say, is to ensure that the military can focus on its primary mission of national defense.
If the armed forces are subjected to overlapping investigations and political pressure, they warn, the military risks becoming an institution that looks to the government's political interests rather than serving the public as a professional force.
The government must recognize the potential consequences of declining morale within the armed forces, critics say.
Dragging the military into political conflict, they warn, could ultimately weaken national security.
-- Reported by Asia Today; translated by UPI
